newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil and U.S. in race row over child's visa.
newsitem.headline: Brazil and U.S. in race row over child's visa.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Monday demanded the U.S. consulate in Rio de Janeiro explain its denial of a visa for a black Brazilian boy, which the American mission denied was a case of racial discrimination.

Newspapers said 6-year-old Carlos Alexandre Carvalho Rossi, who had planned to join other Brazilian schoolchildren on an English language trip to the United States, was denied the visa for race reasons. The other 12 children booked to fly to Florida in January, all white, were granted entry visas.

"The Foreign Ministry requested an informal explanation from the consulate as to why the visa was denied," a spokesman said, stressing that Brazil considered the granting of visas by the United States a "wholly sovereign" affair.

But the U.S. consulate said in a statement Rossi's parents had not made clear in their visa application that the boy was going on a language course and had requested only a tourist visa. It added the parents failed at a later date to provide proof Rossi was to study English.

"The visa was denied according to U.S. visa regulations and not on the grounds of the child's race," the statement said. "We regret that this fact has been incorrectly represented in the media as racial discrimination, which we emphatically state is not the case."

Privately, U.S. diplomatic sources said Ambassador Melvyn Levitsky was furious at the controversy, which coincided with the arrival on Monday of U.S. black leader Jesse Jackson at the start of a "Black Consciousness Week" in Brazil.
The sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Levitsky had also damanded a full account from the Rio de Janeiro consulate and had taken the incident up personally.

Newspapers said Rossi, child of a black mother and white father, was denied a visa because he was an "illegal immigrant threat." His father, Luis Carlos Rossi, a tax official, told the Jornal do Brasil newspaper he intended to demand a formal apology from the U.S. Consulate General.

Ricardo Oliveira Lima, administrative director of Dice English Course, which organised the language trip, accused the U.S. consulate in Rio of "benign" racism. "We've been running a cultural exchange programme for seven years and the only children ever to have their visas denied were coloured," Lima told O Globo newspaper.
Brazilian diplomats said they believed the incident could probably be put down to bureaucracy.

Jackson was to meet President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in Brasilia on Wednesday and to travel later in the week to Rio where local rights campaigners said they hoped to enlist his support in the visa squabble.
